items.title: Market Reversal: Tech Selloff Overwhelms Post-Election Rally
points: Nasdaq down 3.4% for the week; semiconductor giants Micron, Intel, and AMD lost roughly 25% on AI policy fears following Democrats' midterm sweep of Congress.
Nasdaq Composite (a market index weighted toward technology companies) entered correction territory, down 10%+ from recent highs.
S&P 500, Nasdaq, and Dow all posted worst single-day losses since April 2025, erasing post-election rally gains.
Investors cited fears of AI regulation (artificial intelligence oversight by Congress) as the primary driver of tech weakness.

items.title: Economic Data: Jobs Strong but Services Growth Slows
points: October nonfarm payrolls (total U.S. private and government jobs added) rose by 165,000, more than double forecasts, signaling a resilient labor market.
ISM Services growth index ticked down in October as new order growth slowed, hinting at softening in the broader services economy.
Mixed data complicates Fed outlook: strong jobs support further tightening while services slowdown suggests spreading weakness.
CME FedWatch Tool now prices a 77.1% probability of a 25 basis point (0.25%) rate hike at the December FOMC meeting.

items.title: Sector-Specific Carnage: Hardware and Energy Hit Hardest
points: Semiconductors (computer chips) fell sharply: Micron, Lam Research, Intel, and AMD all lost about 25% on AI-related demand concerns.
Energy sector dropped 11.9% for the week as WTI crude fell 13.2% to $90.50/barrel and Brent fell 13.7% to $97.94/barrel.
Information Technology was the worst-performing S&P 500 sector, down 6.9% for the week, while Consumer Staples and Utilities posted small gains.
Storage/memory makers Seagate, Marvell, Western Digital, and Sandisk all fell 27-28% on weakening demand outlook.

items.title: Global Market Impact and Volatility Surge
points: International markets diverged: Japan fell 9.3%, while Hong Kong gained 5.1% and India surged 8.8%.
CBOE Volatility Index (VIX), a measure of expected stock market swings, spiked 32% to 25.64, indicating elevated investor fear.
Relative U.S. economic strength versus global weakness produced uneven sector impacts, hitting tech hardest while sparing some defensive names.

items.title: Individual Stock Moves: Winners and Losers
points: AppLovin (APP) surged 71% and Fiserv (FISV) gained 26%, bucking the broader tech selloff.
Lumentum Holdings (LITE) fell 36%; Seagate, Marvell, and Western Digital each fell about 28% on storage/optical demand concerns.
Apple, Palantir, and Qualcomm reported earnings during the selloff but faced sector-wide repricing headwinds.
Financials sector gained 1.1%, holding up better as rate hike expectations could boost bank net interest margins (the profit spread between lending and deposit rates).

items.title: Week's Bottom Line
points: S&P 500 closed the week -2.7%, Nasdaq -3.4%, Dow -0.9%, with tech bearing the brunt of rotation out of AI and semiconductor plays.
Strong jobs data and persistent rate hike expectations set the stage for continued tightening into year-end.
Oil's collapse reflects demand destruction concerns amid growth slowdown fears, while gold gained 4.6% as a safe-haven play.
Upcoming catalysts include earnings from Adobe and other mega-caps, plus continued repricing of rate expectations.

headlines: Stock market suffered worst day in 18 months as tech stocks collapsed: Nasdaq down 3.4% for the week, with semiconductor giants like Micron, Intel, and AMD losing 25% on AI policy fears following Democrats' midterm election sweep of Congress.
October jobs report beat expectations with 165,000 new nonfarm payrolls added—more than double forecasts—while ISM Services growth slowed, signaling mixed economic signals heading into year-end.
Oil prices plummeted 13% on the week as crude dropped to $90.50/barrel and Brent fell to $97.94, weighing heavily on energy sector which lost 11.9% for the week.
Interest rate hike probability climbed to 77.1% for December FOMC meeting (a basis point is 0.01% change in interest rates), adding to investor uncertainty about Fed policy ahead.
Major indices posted worst one-day losses since April 2025: S&P 500 down 2.7%, Nasdaq entered correction territory down 10%+ from highs, and Dow erased all post-election rally gains.

sections.title: 1. Market Reversal: Tech Selloff Overwhelms Post-Election Rally
points: Markets soared after Democrats won control of both House and Senate on Nov. 6, but reversed sharply within days as technology and semiconductor stocks became targets of a sustained selloff.
Nasdaq Composite (a market index weighted toward technology companies) fell into correction territory—down 10% from its recent peak—signaling formal start of a market downturn in that sector.
All three major indexes (S&P 500, Nasdaq, Dow) posted worst single-day losses since April 2025, erasing the post-midterm optimism that had briefly boosted market sentiment.
Investors cited policy fears related to AI regulation (artificial intelligence oversight by Congress) as the primary driver of tech sector weakness throughout the week.

sections.title: 2. Economic Data: Jobs Strong but Services Growth Slows
points: October nonfarm payrolls (total U.S. private and government jobs added) jumped by 165,000, more than double what economists expected, suggesting labor market remains resilient.
ISM Services growth index declined month-over-month, with new order growth slowing, indicating potential weakness emerging in the broader services economy.
Mixed signals complicate Federal Reserve outlook: strong job creation supports argument for continued rate hikes, while services slowdown suggests economic weakness may be spreading.
CME FedWatch Tool now prices in 77.1% probability the Fed raises rates by 25 basis points (0.25%) at December meeting, up from previous estimates.

sections.title: 3. Sector-Specific Carnage: Hardware and Energy Hit Hardest
points: Semiconductors (computer chips) experienced severe declines: Micron (MU), Lam Research (LRCX), Intel (INTC), and AMD all lost roughly 25% as investors fled tech hardware on AI concerns.
Energy sector collapsed 11.9% for the week amid crude oil drop: WTI crude futures fell 13.2% to $90.50/barrel, and Brent crude dropped 13.7% to $97.94/barrel.
Information Technology sector as a whole plunged 6.9% for the week, the worst performing S&P 500 sector, while traditional defensive sectors (Consumer Staples, Utilities) posted small gains.
Storage and memory makers like Seagate (STX), Marvell Technology (MRVL), Western Digital (WDC), and Sandisk (SNDK) all fell 27-28% on weakening demand outlook.

sections.title: 4. Global Market Impact and Volatility Surge
points: International markets showed mixed results: Japan fell 9.3% (weakness spreading globally), while Hong Kong gained 5.1% and India surged 8.8%, reflecting regional divergence.
CBOE Volatility Index (VIX)—a measure of expected stock market swings—spiked 32% to 25.64, indicating substantially elevated investor fear and uncertainty.
U.S. economic strength relative to global weakness created uneven impact: broad-based selloff in tech but some resilience in defensive and economically-sensitive sectors.

sections.title: 5. Individual Stock Moves: Winners and Losers
points: AppLovin (APP) surged 71% and Fiserv (FISV) gained 26%, bucking broader tech weakness with strong earnings or strategic developments.
Major losers included Lumentum Holdings (LITE) down 36%, Seagate (STX), Marvell (MRVL), and Western Digital (WDC) all down 28%, as storage and optical communications demand concerns spread.
Apple (AAPL), Palantir (PLTR), and Qualcomm (QCOM) reported earnings during the selloff but faced headwinds from sector-wide repricing and policy uncertainty.
Financial stocks held up relatively better: Financials sector gained 1.1% as rate hike expectations may eventually benefit bank net interest margins (profit spread between lending and deposit rates).

sections.title: 6. Week's Bottom Line
points: S&P 500 closed -2.7% for the week, Nasdaq -3.4%, Dow -0.9%, with tech sector bearing the brunt of rotation out of high-flying AI and semiconductor plays.
Strong October jobs data and persistent rate hike expectations set stage for continued policy tightening, potentially weighing on growth stocks into year-end.
Oil collapse reflects demand destruction concerns amid growth slowdown, while gold gained 4.6% as traditional safe-haven asset as investors sought protection.
For week ahead, major catalysts include earnings from Adobe and other mega-cap companies, plus continued market repricing of rate expectations based on economic data flow.
